name: Agricultural Advocacy & Literacy

objectives.text: Identify the farm or natural resource source of common foods, fibers, and everyday products
Identify common misconceptions people have about farming and food production
Describe how agriculture supplies the food, fiber, fuel, and shelter that families use every day
Explain why agricultural literacy matters to consumers who are not farmers
Distinguish between fact and opinion in claims made about food and farming
Explain what common food label claims such as organic, non-GMO, and hormone-free mean and what they do not mean
Explain how honesty and respect for others should shape the way an agriculturalist speaks about farming and food
Demonstrate explaining the farm-to-table journey of a food product to someone unfamiliar with agriculture
Compare agricultural literacy, which informs the public, with agricultural advocacy, which seeks to persuade
Explain how agricultural education and the FFA build agricultural literacy in the school and community
Summarize the role and economic scope of agriculture, food, and natural resources in society using data suitable for a public audience
Evaluate the credibility of sources of agricultural information such as extension publications, USDA data, industry groups, and social media posts
Analyze a media portrayal of agriculture for accuracy and bias
Analyze public concerns about a modern production technology such as GE crops or precision agriculture against scientific evidence and USDA sustainable practices criteria
Compare conventional, organic, and other alternative production systems fairly when explaining food choices to consumers
Plan and teach an agricultural literacy lesson to elementary students
Apply audience analysis and shared-values communication strategies when discussing a controversial agricultural topic with a skeptical consumer
Analyze how a current public policy issue affects agricultural producers and identify the stakeholders on each side
Develop an advocacy presentation correcting a common misconception about modern agriculture
Create accurate and ethical social media content that tells a personal agricultural or SAE story to a general audience
Construct a written or spoken policy position on an agricultural issue addressed to an elected official
Design and lead an agricultural literacy campaign for a school or community audience
Evaluate the effectiveness of an agricultural literacy campaign using audience feedback and measurable outcomes

changes: Kept all six original competencies, rewording the grade 8 practice objective to an observable verb and splitting the grade 12 campaign objective into separate design and evaluation competencies. Added foundational literacy objectives for the lower grades (food and fiber sources, agriculture in daily life, fact versus opinion, food label claims, honest speech). Added high school competencies for literacy versus advocacy, the role of agricultural education and FFA, the economic scope of agriculture, source credibility, technology concerns, production system comparison, teaching elementary lessons, audience-centered dialogue, policy analysis and policy communication, and social media storytelling. Anchored high school objectives only to AFNR standards they actually teach and left sibling material on CDEs, service projects, and career networking out.
